title: Question 2: Collective Bargaining for CPCS Employees

context.text: Placed on the ballot by initiative petition: the Information for Voters labels it a law proposed by initiative petition on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026. The Legislature's Special Joint Committee on Initiative Petitions issued the legislative reports reproduced in the same booklet.

question.text: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? Collective Bargaining for CPCS Employees: This proposed law would specify that employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services (“CPCS”) are permitted to engage in collective bargaining with their employer. It would also require CPCS, after executing a collective bargaining agreement, to request the appropriation necessary to fund such agreement from the Governor.

summary.text: The measure would specify that employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services (CPCS) may engage in collective bargaining with their employer, and would require CPCS, after executing a collective bargaining agreement, to request the necessary appropriation from the Governor. Statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office for Administration and Finance): The proposed law may have an impact on state finances. CPCS receives its funding, in part, from state government appropriations. The fiscal impact of the proposed law is difficult to project due to the uncertainty regarding the outcomes of any such collective bargaining by CPCS employees.

measure.yesMeans: A YES VOTE would specify that Committee for Public Counsel Services employees may form a union to collectively bargain with their employer.
measure.noMeans: A NO VOTE would make no change to the law governing labor relations for Committee for Public Counsel Service employees.

argumentsFor.text: In the 150-word argument in favor signed by Tom McKeever of Labor Unions for Public Counsel Workers Rights, as printed in the Information for Voters: "A YES vote will give employees of the Massachusetts Committee for Public Counsel Services (CPCS) the right to organize a union and collectively bargain with their employer if they choose to do so."

researchNotes: Ballot text, official yes/no statements and fiscal statements are taken from the Secretary of the Commonwealth's 2026 Information for Voters booklet (PDF text extracted and checked by script). Arguments are quoted from the signed 150-word pro/con statements, which the Commonwealth states reflect the authors' opinions and are not certified as accurate. No signed argument against appears: the booklet states there was no organized group urging a No vote and prints text compiled by the Secretary's office, which is not quoted here. The booklet's own summary is the Attorney General's; the Secretary's page and Ballotpedia could not be fetched (bot protection), so the ballot list was confirmed from the booklet itself, which covers nine questions.
